Voglio, posso, devo

Like their English counterparts (want, can, must), these three verbs are irregular and are followed by an infinitive. You'll use them all the time: to say what you want, what you can and what you have to do.

volere (to want)potere (can, to be able)dovere (must, to have to)
iovogliopossodevo
tuvuoipuoidevi
lui, leivuolepuòdeve
noivogliamopossiamodobbiamo
voivoletepotetedovete
lorovoglionopossonodevono

The trick for voi: start from the infinitive, drop -re and add -te. vole-re → volete, pote-re → potete, dove-re → dovete. So for dovere it's dovete, with an o: “devete” and “debbete” don't exist.

The traps to watch for

  • I want = voglio, never “vuo”: Voglio andare a casa.
  • You (plural) must = dovete (with o), but you must (one friend) = devi and he must = deve (with e).
  • We must = dobbiamo, with a double b.
  • He can = può, with an accent on the o.
", "

+ infinitive, and asking politely

The second verb stays in the infinitive and follows directly, with no preposition. Careful: English says “I want to go”, but Italian has no “to” here, and you never add a or di. Only the first verb is conjugated.

Devo lavorare. Non posso venire.I have to work. I can't come.

The negation non goes before the conjugated verb, like “not” but placed in front: Non voglio uscire.

To ask for something

You want to…You say
ask for permissionPosso entrare? Posso provare? Posso andare in bagno?
ask a friend for a favorPuoi aiutare Marco?
ask a favor formally (to a stranger)Può ripetere, per favore?
invite someoneVuoi venire con noi?
say politely what you'd likeVorrei prenotare un tavolo.

To address one person formally, Italian uses the 3rd person singular (Lei): Può ripetere? means “Could you repeat that?” said to a stranger. To several people, you say potete.

Voglio un caffè is correct, but it sounds a bit blunt at the bar, just like “I want a coffee” in English. To be polite, use vorrei (I would like): Vorrei un caffè, per favore.

title: Want, can, must
topic: volere, potere, dovere + infinitive; asking politely
why: After andare, venire, uscire and fare, dire, stare, dare, here are the three verbs that let you say what you want, can and have to do. Learners write “debbete / devete” for dovete and “vuo andare” for voglio andare: this lesson locks in those forms, the direct infinitive (no “to”) and the polite requests you need when traveling and with friends.
